summaries.example: Imagine a small wooden ship in a tank of water. It is a scale model of a real ship. It can help engineers study how water pushes against the ship. But the small ship is not exactly like the real one: its size and materials are different. Scientists must figure out which results can be carried over.
summaries.summary: Scientists use models as tools for studying things that may be too large, small, complicated, dangerous, or difficult to investigate directly. A model might be a physical copy, such as a small ship; an analogy, such as comparing gas particles with billiard balls; an imagined object, such as a frictionless pendulum; an equation; or a computer simulation. Models represent selected features of a target system, not every feature. They often use idealizations, which are purposeful simplifications or distortions. These changes can make a problem easier to investigate, although they also create questions about what conclusions are safe. Philosophers ask what models are, how they represent, how scientists learn from them, and whether models belong to a theory or can work independently. Models can help scientists discover patterns, test ideas, explain behavior, and gain understanding. Because models have strengths and limits, scientists often compare several models and balance accuracy, simplicity, and general usefulness.
key_ideas: Models can be physical objects, imagined objects, drawings, descriptions, equations, or computer programs.
A model usually represents only some parts or features of its target. No model copies everything perfectly.
Scientists use models to explore possibilities, make predictions, explain patterns, and understand difficult systems.
A model may simplify or even deliberately distort reality so that an important pattern is easier to study.
Scientists build, test, compare, manipulate, and revise models rather than simply accepting them as final answers.
Different models of the same thing may be useful for different purposes, even when they do not agree in every detail.
summaries.why_it_matters: Models are part of how science works, from studying atoms and living populations to examining economies and climate. Knowing that a model is a tool—not a perfect copy—helps us use scientific information carefully. It also explains why scientists can use a simple or partly false model without thinking that every detail of it is real.

important_terms.definition: A model is something scientists build, imagine, or calculate to study a system or part of the world.
The real thing, event, or process that a model is meant to help us study.
A model that copies some features of something else, such as its shape or relationships.
A useful simplification or change made to a complicated situation.
Learning about a real system by first studying a model that stands in for it.

questions_to_think_about: What parts of a real thing should a model include?
When could a simple model teach us more clearly than a very detailed one?
If two models disagree, could both still be useful?
How can we tell whether a model's results apply to its target?
What might be lost when scientists simplify a complicated system?

summaries.example: Consider a model of predator–prey populations. It may use equations describing how prey increase and predators reduce the prey population. The model can reveal cycles of growth and decline even though no actual ecosystem follows the equations exactly. Its value may be exploratory or explanatory rather than predictive. Researchers must still ask which biological features the model leaves out and why its conclusions should apply to a particular ecosystem.
summaries.summary: Models occupy a central but philosophically complicated place in science. They are used to represent target systems, yet representation is not simply a matter of copying: a model selects features, uses analogies or structures, and may introduce deliberate distortions. The entry surveys models as physical objects, imagined or fictional objects, abstract artifacts, mathematical structures, descriptions, and equations. It also distinguishes model types by their roles. Scale models preserve some physical relations; analogical models use relevant similarities; idealized and toy models simplify or distort; minimal models may appear to lack ordinary similarity; exploratory models generate possibilities; and data models organize corrected and fitted observations. These models support learning about both the model and its target, as well as explanation, understanding, theory construction, and prediction. Philosophers disagree about how such functions are possible when models are false or idealized. They also debate whether models are merely interpretations of theories or autonomous tools that mediate between theories and the world. These issues connect modeling with scientific realism, laws, reduction, emergence, and the trade-offs among accuracy, simplicity, and generality.
key_ideas: The semantics of modeling concerns representation: models select and organize features of a target, but the general nature of representation remains philosophically disputed.
The ontology of models is pluralistic. Scientific models may be material objects, fictional or abstract objects, structures, descriptions, equations, or combinations of these.
Idealized, toy, minimal, analogical, exploratory, phenomenological, surrogate, and data models serve different purposes; these categories can overlap.
Models support knowledge by being constructed and manipulated. Computer simulations can reveal consequences that analytic methods cannot easily derive, while also introducing methodological risks.
There is disagreement about whether models explain because they preserve relevant causal structure, because their distortions isolate important patterns, or in other ways.
Models may be subordinate to theories, complements to them, preliminary tools, or autonomous mediators. In complex research, the boundary between model and theory may be unclear.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding models helps explain why science can make progress with representations that are selective, simplified, and sometimes inconsistent with one another. It also encourages careful reasoning about what a model establishes and what requires additional evidence. The philosophical study of models shows that scientific practice involves construction, interpretation, comparison, and judgment—not just deduction from finished theories.

important_terms.definition: A model's relation to a selected part, process, or aspect of the world that it is used to investigate.
The system, phenomenon, or data that a model is intended to stand for or illuminate.
A deliberate simplification or distortion introduced to make a system more tractable or intelligible.
A quantitative relation in which one description is close to another in a specified mathematical sense.
An account of models as structures, often mathematical or set-theoretic, that satisfy or interpret a formal theory.
Reasoning about a target by constructing, manipulating, and evaluating a model of it.
The view that models can operate with some freedom from theories and can connect theories with real-world systems.

questions_to_think_about: Can a model represent a target if it shares very little with that target?
When does an idealization clarify a causal pattern, and when might it mislead?
Could two incompatible models both be successful because they capture different perspectives or purposes?
What makes evidence from a surrogate model transferable to its target?
Should scientific models be judged mainly by truth, prediction, explanation, understanding, or a balance among these aims?

summaries.example: Suppose a class uses a computer model of a town to study traffic. The program may represent roads, cars, and traffic lights, but it may leave out weather, accidents, and many differences between drivers. By changing one rule at a time, students can see how traffic jams might form. The model does not predict every real traffic event. It helps explore patterns and possible explanations.
summaries.summary: Scientific models are tools for representing and investigating parts of the world. They can be objects in a laboratory, imagined systems, mathematical structures, equations, written descriptions, or computer programs. Their targets include things such as atoms, populations, economies, and climate systems. A model never needs to copy every feature of its target. A scale model may preserve shape but not material; an analogical model may preserve relationships; an idealized model may simplify or distort; and a data model may turn messy observations into a cleaner pattern. These choices can make difficult questions manageable, but they also limit what the model can show. Scientists learn by building and manipulating models, then deciding how results about the model bear on the target. Philosophers debate whether models are fictional objects, abstract objects, structures, descriptions, or combinations of these. They also debate whether models are mainly parts of theories or whether they have their own independence. Models may help apply theories, explore theories, develop new ideas, explain patterns, and provide understanding. Since no single model normally maximizes accuracy, simplicity, and generality at once, scientists often compare models and choose according to their purpose.
key_ideas: Scientists use many kinds of models, including physical replicas, imagined objects, equations, structures, descriptions, and computer simulations.
A model is selective. It may show shape, relationships, or a pattern while ignoring other features.
Some models are idealized: they assume things such as no friction, perfect rationality, or complete isolation, even when those assumptions are not literally true.
Models can be used to learn, explain, predict, explore possible situations, and understand theories.
Philosophers disagree about what a model really is. Some compare models with fictional objects, while others treat them as abstract structures or descriptions.
Models can be connected to theories in different ways. They may apply a theory, fill in details that a theory leaves open, or help when no useful theory is available.
summaries.why_it_matters: Models are everywhere in science, but calling something a model does not guarantee that it is true or complete. Learning how models represent and simplify helps us ask better questions about scientific claims. It also shows why a model that is poor at exact prediction might still be useful for exploring a mechanism or making a complicated idea understandable.

important_terms.definition: A tool used to study a real thing or process by standing for selected parts of it.
The real object, process, or situation that a model is meant to represent.
The way a model stands for or gives information about its target.
A planned simplification or distortion that makes a complicated problem easier to study.
A similarity between two systems that helps one system teach us about another.
A cleaned-up and organized version of observations, often made by removing errors and fitting a pattern.
A model that can work with some independence from a theory and help connect theory with the world.

questions_to_think_about: Why might scientists choose a model that is known to be unrealistic?
What is the difference between using an analogy and using a physical copy?
How should scientists decide which observations to remove when making a model of data?
Can a model explain something even if some of its assumptions are false?
Why might scientists keep several models of the same target?
